item.research_question: Why does the Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) exhibit higher ballistic resistance than the Mn-containing Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi), and what are the underlying deformation mechanisms during high-speed impact?
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with 2NN MEAM potential; ballistic impact simulated by a 3 nm iron rigid sphere at 25 nm/ps; uniaxial tension at strain rates of 5 × 10^7, 5 × 10^8, and 5 × 10^9 s^-1; temperatures of 70 K, 300 K, and 1000 K.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature (300 K) for ballistic impact; high strain rates (10^7 to 10^9 s^-1); plate thicknesses of 2.29 nm and 6.04 nm; bullet speed 25 nm/ps.
key_findings: The Mn-free HEA (CrFeCoNi) blocked the high-speed sphere at a smaller penetration depth (2 ps) compared to the Mn-containing HEA (2.5 ps).
The Mn-free HEA exhibited stronger interatomic bonding with a cohesive energy of -4.25 eV per atom, versus -4.01 eV per atom for the Mn-containing alloy.
Higher strain rates induced more active dislocations, significantly enhancing the strain hardening and toughness of the Mn-free HEA.
Dislocation tangling occurred earlier and more easily in the Mn-containing HEA due to Mn's larger atomic radius causing lattice distortion.
The Mn-containing HEA showed more amorphization and structural damage throughout the plate, while the Mn-free HEA maintained better structural integrity.
Deformation twinning was not a dominant factor at room temperature; planar-slip dislocations played the predominant role in plastic deformation.
The Mn-free HEA had a lower stacking fault energy (more negative) than the Mn-containing HEA, favoring the dissociation of full dislocations into partial dislocations.
item.mechanism: The superior ballistic resistance of CrFeCoNi is attributed to its stronger interatomic bonding (due to Mn's lower electron work function in CrMnFeCoNi) and higher dislocation density generated at high strain rates. In CrFeCoNi, energy is absorbed by activating dislocations and strain hardening, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, weaker bonding and easier dislocation tangling lead to bond breaking, amorphization, and severe structural damage.
item.limitations: The MD simulation dimensions (nanometers) are significantly smaller than real-world ballistic tests (millimeters to centimeters), which may limit the space for dislocation development, though the authors argue this does not affect the calculated influence of Mn on bonding strength.
item.future_work: Sufficient attention needs to be given to the modification of the atomic bonding strength in addition to the plastic deformation mechanism when designing armor and energy-absorption HEAs and related materials.
quotes: Stronger atomic bonding and higher dislocation densities make the CrFeCoNi easier to be strain hardened with elevated toughness to resist high-speed deformation
The Mn-free HEA has higher elastic modulus with stronger atomic bonding, which is consistent with experimental measurements

Dislocation tangling is found to occur earlier in the Mn-containing HEA when higher strain rates are applied, but its weaker atomic bonding due to the presence of Mn makes the structural integrity of CrMnFeCoNi easier to be damaged
